sourceCheck: Pinned to GNU Bash 5.3 with official patches 001-020. The successfully opened [GNU Bash release directory](https://ftp.gnu.org/pub/gnu/bash/) and [5.3 patch directory](https://ftp.gnu.org/pub/gnu/bash/bash-5.3-patches/) list 5.3 as the newest stable series and bash53-020 as its highest patch; no newer stable series or patch is listed. FTP timestamps are treated as upload metadata. Successfully opened Chet Ramey's [July 5, 2025 release announcement and included NEWS](https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/bug-bash/2025-07/msg00005.html), the [upstream Bash man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/bash.1.html), and [signal(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal.7.html). The GNU reference manual at https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/bash.html and attempted relevant subsection pages timed out, so matching man-page sections provide the behavior verification. Inspected the requested quoting, parameters, expansions, functions, arrays, conditions, loops, arithmetic, pipelines, lists, redirections, execution environments, statuses, signals, set and shopt coverage, including getopts, read, local, declare, return, exit, wait and trap individually. No section scope remains unverified using that fallback. man7 identifies GNU Bash 5.3, but its COLOPHON says it came from upstream Git on 2026-08-03, with the latest commit dated 2026-06-10; it is not a release snapshot. The release NEWS confirms the current-environment command substitutions, including the REPLY form, GLOBSORT pathname ordering, array_expand_once replacing assoc_expand_once, and changed parenthesized multiargument test parsing that remains ambiguous. The matching man entries confirm those features and mark assoc_expand_once deprecated. The announcement's summary says pathname completion for GLOBSORT, whereas its included NEWS and the man page identify pathname expansion; the deck follows the latter. NEWS lists a none sorting selector while the current man page documents nosort; neither disputed selector appears in the plan or cards. Release-sensitive features used here are confirmed as released in 5.3; deprecated test parsing puzzles are omitted.

cards.statement: With x=ready, Bash passes 'value=$x' as the argument value=ready.
cards.explanation: Single quotes preserve the literal $x, so the argument is value=$x.
cards.misconception: Single quotes expand variable references.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting

cards.statement: With x='a b', Bash passes "$x" as one command argument containing a b.
cards.explanation: Double quotes keep the expanded space inside the argument.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting and Word Splitting

cards.statement: Bash passes $'a\tb' as one argument with a tab between a and b.
cards.explanation: ANSI-C quoting decodes \t before Bash supplies the argument.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting

cards.statement: Bash removes the backslash from "a\q" when forming its argument.
cards.explanation: A backslash before q stays literal inside double quotes, so the argument contains a backslash between a and q.
cards.misconception: Double quotes strip a backslash before any character.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting

cards.statement: Bash parses a\ b as one command argument containing a space.
cards.explanation: The unquoted backslash quotes the following space, keeping it inside the word.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting

cards.statement: With x=mid, Bash expands pre"$x"'post' into the single argument premidpost.
cards.explanation: Adjacent quoted and unquoted parts belong to the same word.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting and Expansion

cards.statement: With IFS=' ' and x=' a ', Bash gives empty arguments around a when expanding unquoted $x.
cards.explanation: Bash discards IFS whitespace at the edges; this expansion supplies the argument a.
cards.misconception: Edge spaces produce empty fields during word splitting.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Word Splitting

cards.statement: With IFS=: and x=a::b, Bash gives an empty argument between a and b when expanding unquoted $x.
cards.explanation: Adjacent non-whitespace IFS delimiters produce an empty field.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Word Splitting

cards.statement: With IFS='' and x='a b', Bash splits unquoted $x into separate a and b arguments.
cards.explanation: An empty IFS disables word splitting, leaving a b as one argument.
cards.misconception: An empty IFS restores the usual space delimiters.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Word Splitting

cards.statement: With x='', Bash passes "" $x to a command as two empty arguments.
cards.explanation: The explicit "" survives; the unquoted empty expansion disappears, leaving one empty argument.
cards.misconception: An unquoted empty scalar preserves an argument just like explicit empty quotes.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Word Splitting

cards.statement: With positional parameters 'a b' and '', Bash forwards each intact through "$@".
cards.explanation: Quoted "$@" produces one argument per positional parameter, preserving the empty parameter.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Special Parameters

cards.statement: With IFS=':,' and positional parameters a and b, Bash expands "$*" to the single argument a:,b.
cards.explanation: Quoted "$*" uses the first IFS character between values, producing a:b.
cards.misconception: Quoted "$*" uses the entire IFS value as its separator.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Special Parameters

cards.statement: With x='*.cfg', Bash applies pathname expansion after splitting unquoted $x.
cards.explanation: An unquoted expansion can supply a glob pattern for the later pathname-expansion stage.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Expansion

cards.statement: With x=';', Bash treats the semicolon produced by $x as a command separator.
cards.explanation: Bash recognizes command syntax before expansion; the expanded semicolon is ordinary argument text.
cards.misconception: Expansion output becomes shell control syntax.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Shell Grammar and Expansion

cards.statement: With n=3, Bash expands {1..$n} into the words 1 2 3.
cards.explanation: Brace expansion runs before parameter expansion, so $n does not become a sequence endpoint.
cards.misconception: Brace sequences evaluate variable endpoints.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Brace Expansion

cards.statement: Bash expands {b,a} into b followed by a in the written order.
cards.explanation: Brace expansion generates textual alternatives in their written order.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Brace Expansion

cards.statement: With HOME=/srv/me, Bash expands "~/cfg" into /srv/me/cfg.
cards.explanation: The quoted tilde stays literal, so this argument is ~/cfg.
cards.misconception: A tilde inside double quotes expands like an unquoted tilde.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Tilde Expansion

cards.statement: With x='a *', Bash stores a * literally when it executes the scalar assignment value=$x.
cards.explanation: Scalar assignment values skip word splitting and pathname expansion.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameters

cards.statement: With nullglob enabled, Bash removes an unmatched unquoted *.cfg argument from a command.
cards.explanation: An unmatched pattern disappears from the command's argument list when nullglob is enabled.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pathname Expansion

cards.statement: With failglob enabled, Bash runs a command with an unmatched *.cfg pattern as a literal argument.
cards.explanation: failglob reports an expansion error and prevents that command from executing.
cards.misconception: failglob leaves an unmatched pattern as literal argument text.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pathname Expansion

cards.statement: With dotglob enabled and .env present, Bash includes .env among the matches for *.
cards.explanation: dotglob permits * to match the initial dot in .env.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pathname Expansion

cards.statement: With globskipdots enabled, Bash excludes . and .. when expanding the pattern .*.
cards.explanation: globskipdots filters the two special directory entries even when the pattern starts with a dot.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pathname Expansion

cards.statement: In Bash 5.3, GLOBSORT=-name makes Bash sort pathname matches in ascending name order.
cards.explanation: The leading minus reverses the name sort, so -name selects descending order.
cards.misconception: A leading minus in GLOBSORT preserves ascending order.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: GLOBSORT

cards.statement: Bash performs quote removal before pathname expansion when preparing a command's arguments.
cards.explanation: Quote removal is the final expansion stage, after pathname expansion.
cards.misconception: Bash removes quoting before it expands pathname patterns.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Expansion

cards.statement: With x='', Bash expands ${x-fallback} to the empty value stored in x.
cards.explanation: A null value still counts as set. Adding a colon to -, =, ? or + makes that operator test null values too.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x=ready, Bash runs printf in ${x:-$(printf fallback)} before returning x's value.
cards.explanation: Bash selects ready and leaves the unused fallback unexpanded, so its command substitution does not run.
cards.misconception: Bash evaluates fallback words even when it selects the existing value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x='', Bash assigns ready to x when it evaluates ${x:=ready}.
cards.explanation: The := form stores its fallback in an unset or empty variable.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x='', Bash expands ${x:?missing} to missing and continues the command.
cards.explanation: In a noninteractive shell, :? reports the supplied error text and exits with a nonzero status.
cards.misconception: The error operator supplies its message as an ordinary fallback value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x=ready, Bash expands ${x:+enabled} to the existing value ready.
cards.explanation: The :+ form selects its alternate word, so this expansion produces enabled.
cards.misconception: The alternate-value operator returns the existing parameter value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: Bash's ${#x} expansion counts characters in the scalar x, including spaces.
cards.explanation: The length belongs to the scalar's value rather than the number of words it could form.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x=abcdef, Bash expands ${x: -2} to the initial two characters ab.
cards.explanation: A negative substring offset counts from the end; this expansion yields ef.
cards.misconception: A negative substring offset selects characters from the beginning.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x=a/b/c, Bash expands ${x##*/} to the remaining text b/c.
cards.explanation: The ## form removes the longest matching prefix, a/b/, leaving c; # chooses the shortest match.
cards.misconception: The doubled prefix-removal operator chooses the shortest matching prefix.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x=a.b.c, Bash expands ${x%.*} to the remaining text a.b.
cards.explanation: The % form removes the shortest matching suffix, .c; %% chooses the longest match.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x=banana, Bash expands ${x//a/X} to bXnXnX by replacing the matching a characters.
cards.explanation: The doubled slash applies the replacement to each matching a in the value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With x=ab, Bash changes x itself to AB when it expands ${x^^}.
cards.explanation: The ^^ expansion yields AB while the stored value of x remains ab.
cards.misconception: Case-modification expansion rewrites the original variable.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: With ordinary scalars x=ready and ref=x, Bash expands ${!ref} to ready.
cards.explanation: Indirect expansion uses ref's value as the name of the parameter to read.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: Bash evaluates the division in $((7 / 2)) using integer arithmetic.
cards.explanation: The arithmetic expansion truncates the integer quotient toward zero.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

cards.statement: Bash requires declare -i before it evaluates a variable's value as an arithmetic expression.
cards.explanation: An arithmetic operand's value is evaluated as an expression even when its variable lacks the integer attribute.
cards.misconception: Expression evaluation requires the variable's integer attribute.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

cards.statement: With x='', Bash rejects $((x + 1)) because x holds an empty string.
cards.explanation: A null variable referenced by name evaluates to zero, so this expansion yields 1.
cards.misconception: An empty arithmetic variable makes the expression invalid.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

cards.statement: Bash reads 010 in arithmetic expansion as a decimal integer.
cards.explanation: A leading zero selects octal notation, so 010 represents decimal eight.
cards.misconception: Arithmetic constants with leading zeros remain decimal.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

cards.statement: Bash interprets the digits in $((10#08)) using the explicitly selected decimal base.
cards.explanation: The base#digits notation makes this 08 a valid decimal value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

cards.statement: With n=1, Bash's $((n+=2)) expansion updates n in the current shell.
cards.explanation: Arithmetic assignments inside an expansion modify the referenced variable; n becomes 3.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation and Arithmetic Expansion

cards.statement: With stdout and stderr separate, Bash includes stderr text in the value captured by $(command).
cards.explanation: This substitution captures standard output; standard error keeps its separate destination.
cards.misconception: Command substitution captures both output streams.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

cards.statement: Bash preserves trailing newline characters in the value captured by "$(command)".
cards.explanation: The $(...) form removes trailing newlines from captured standard output, including inside double quotes.
cards.misconception: Quoting a command substitution preserves its trailing newlines.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

cards.statement: Given a readable file f containing abc, Bash expands $(<f) to abc.
cards.explanation: The $(<f) shorthand reads the file's contents into the substitution result.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

cards.statement: Bash accepts $(printf '%s' "$(printf x)") as a nested command substitution.
cards.explanation: The inner substitution supplies x to the outer printf command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

cards.statement: In Bash 5.3, ${ x=changed; printf ok; } leaves x=changed in the calling shell.
cards.explanation: This substitution runs in the current execution environment, so the assignment persists.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

cards.statement: In Bash 5.3, ${| REPLY=ready; printf shown; } expands to shown.
cards.explanation: The ${| ...; } form expands to REPLY, here ready; shown goes to the caller's standard output.
cards.misconception: The REPLY form captures standard output as its expansion result.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution
